tagline: A field guide to the birds of the Western Ghats
about_html:
Birds of the Sahyadris

Birds of the Sahyadris is dedicated to the remarkable birdlife of India’s Western Ghats (the Sahyadris), a UNESCO-recognised global biodiversity hotspot. These mountains support more than 500 bird species – over a third of India’s birdlife – including some of the country’s most distinctive and threatened birds.

About the Project

This guide offers plain-language identification notes for a growing set of Western Ghats species, spanning evergreen forests, shola–grassland mosaics, river valleys, plantations, and hill slopes. Each entry includes practical notes on identification, behaviour, habitat and conservation, paired, where available, with photographs. The project expands over time as more species, images, and insights are added.

Western Ghats: Avian Highlights

  • Over 500 species occur across the range seasonally or year-round, from tiny sunbirds and flowerpeckers to large hornbills and raptors.
  • Around thirty species are endemic to the Western Ghats under current taxonomy – including Malabar Parakeet, Nilgiri Blue Robin, Wayanad Laughingthrush, and Malabar Grey Hornbill.
  • Four of India’s nine hornbills occur in the Western Ghats: the Great, Malabar Pied, Malabar Grey and Indian Grey.
  • Several of India’s most threatened birds – such as the Nilgiri Pipit and Broad-tailed Grassbird – are restricted to high shola–grassland ridges.
  • Over 70 bird families are represented, from bulbuls and babblers to drongos, doves, swifts, raptors, and woodpeckers.
  • Behavioural specialities abound: the Malabar Whistling Thrush can mimic human whistles, and the wingbeats of a Great Hornbill can be heard long before the bird is seen.

Why the Western Ghats Matter

The Western Ghats are an irreplaceable reservoir of India’s avian diversity. Many of their rarest species face mounting pressure from habitat loss, fragmentation, and climate change. This guide aims to support awareness and conservation by making the birds of the Ghats accessible to beginners and experienced birdwatchers alike.

Scientific names follow AviList v2025b (June 2026); conservation categories are the latest published BirdLife/IUCN assessments (2025). Both are versioned data and are refreshed when the checklists change.

This field guide is a work in progress. Your feedback, corrections, and photographs from the Sahyadris are always welcome: please write to mihir [at] naniwadekar [dot] in.
